title: Hanukkah: the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4)
hook: the revolt against Antiochus and the Temple rededicated, told in the books of Maccabees

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakafot, the seven circles of Simchat Torah. Your line was dance with the scroll. Today the calendar jumps ahead, into winter.

A small band of fighters walks up to the Temple in Jerusalem, and stops. The gates are burned. The priests' rooms are torn down. Weeds have grown up in the courtyards, the text says, like a forest or a hillside. The altar has been used for offerings their law forbids. These men have just won battles against a much larger army. And the first thing they do, standing in the ruin, is tear their clothes and put ashes on their heads, the way you'd mourn a death. The story of Hanukkah, in this telling, starts with grief.
screen: `THE GATES ARE BURNED.` → `WEEDS LIKE A FOREST.` → `A STORY THAT STARTS WITH GRIEF.`

segments.voice: The account here is the First Book of Maccabees. It isn't in the Jewish Bible; it was preserved in Greek, and it's part of the Catholic and Orthodox Christian Bibles. The Greek king Antiochus the Fourth ruled the land. He banned Torah study, circumcision and Shabbat, and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. Some Jews went along; others resisted. In the village of Modiin, an old priest named Mattathias refused to offer a pagan sacrifice and fled to the hills with his five sons. One son, Judah, nicknamed the Maccabee, led a guerrilla army. Before one battle, as the book tells it, his men were afraid of the size of the enemy. Judah answered that victory doesn't depend on numbers; strength comes from heaven. Chapter four is the homecoming. They pull down the defiled altar, and then don't know what to do with its stones. So they store them on the Temple mount, the text says, until a prophet should come and tell them. They build a new altar of whole stones, light the lampstand, and on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev dedicate it, with songs and harps and cymbals, for eight days. Judah decrees the days be kept every year. Hanukkah means dedication. Later, the prayer added on Hanukkah thanks God for delivering the many into the hands of the few.
screen: `A BOOK OUTSIDE THE JEWISH BIBLE.` · `ANTIOCHUS BANS THE TORAH.` · `JUDAH: STRENGTH COMES FROM HEAVEN.` · `A NEW ALTAR, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `THE FEW AGAINST THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you care about that feels outnumbered in your life right now: honesty at work, rest in a busy house, a practice nobody around you shares. Hold it the way the Maccabees held those altar stones, carefully, without rushing to decide everything. Breathe with it.
Hanukkah. Dedication: the altar rebuilt and the Temple rededicated, for eight days, in the month of Kislev. Today's word.
Your line: the few against the many. A week that began with guests in the booth ends at a new altar. Day six hundred sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: Hanukkah is kept for eight nights from the twenty-fifth of Kislev, with candles lit each night and the Al HaNissim prayer added to the daily prayers and grace after meals, recalling the Hasmonean victory and the rededication.

notes: All of 1 Maccabees is paraphrased (no public-domain Jewish translation used). Details: gates burned, shrubs growing 'as in a forest', tearing clothes and ashes (4:38–39); stones stored 'until there should come a prophet' (4:46); dedication with songs, harps and cymbals for eight days on 25 Kislev (4:52–59). Verify.
Mattathias' refusal in Modiin is chapter 2; Judah's speech on numbers is 3:18–19.
Dates: Antiochus IV's decrees c. 167 BCE; rededication c. 164 BCE. Kept vague as 'the 160s'.
Description of which Bibles include 1 Maccabees is factual and unranked; check wording.
Al HaNissim's phrase 'the many into the hands of the few' paraphrased.
